title: Transactions: roll back the experiment and verify a fresh read
goal: Distinguish an in-transaction write, rollback and commit using own synthetic catalog items.
prerequisites: onec.p4; P1–P3; explicit contracts, types, collections and failure handling.
outcomes: Explain why writing inside a transaction is not a final persistence claim.
Verify absence after a controlled refusal.
Commit a separate successful operation and retain the failure reason.
sections: One business fact needs one decision

If a request and dependent record must appear together, do not accept them independently. A transaction groups changes into commit or rollback. It does not make the algorithm correct or replace validation. Identify all affected data and require either complete consistency or the previous state.

A transaction groups database changes until commit or rollback. The function generates a unique synthetic name, starts a transaction, writes a card and deliberately raises an exception. Its handler calls ОтменитьТранзакцию. A fresh lookup outside the rolled-back transaction must return an empty reference. A successful write before rollback does not establish final persistence.

Keep explicit transactions short and finish every path. Do not wait for users, network or long reports while holding a transaction. Some platform operations already have a transactional context; understand the call site before nesting another boundary. A nested start is not an independent backup.

A second transaction creates a separately named accepted card and commits it. A fresh lookup compares the resulting reference. Both checks matter: absence of the rejected name does not prove another commit, and an accepted card does not prove the first rollback. No existing catalog items are cleared or modified.

On exception, roll back the transaction you started and propagate the failure with safe diagnostics. Do not continue as if successful. Rollback cannot undo actions outside the transaction, especially files and external requests. Those need another coordination and idempotency protocol.

A database transaction does not undo arbitrary external effects. A sent message, external file write or third-party HTTP request is not promised to disappear after rollback. This experiment uses no real network or other people’s data. Integration needs delivery protocols, journals, idempotency and agreed compensation, introduced later.

In a separate copy, inject failure between two related writes. Reopen a session and compare both tables after rejection. Then run the valid operation and expect exactly one effect. A before-state snapshot is essential because test setup itself may have changed the baseline.

The incorrect variant replaces rollback in the first error handler with commit. It compiles but retains the rejected item, so the absence assertion becomes false. Do not delete it to conceal the outcome; keep that experiment in its separate copy. A single file-base test does not establish concurrent server transactions or nested-transaction correctness.

mistakes: A successful write before rollback is treated as final persistence.
Reread after completing the transaction using a separate lookup.
The failure branch commits instead of rolling back.
Review each ending branch and independently assert absence of the rejected change.
Database rollback is assumed to reverse external HTTP effects.
Separate database state from external effects and specify delivery/compensation.
